notes.definition: Many drugs were first extracted from plants and microorganisms, but most new drugs are now made by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry. Every new drug must pass preclinical testing and clinical trials to check that it is safe and effective before it can be used.
explanation: Traditionally, drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves. The painkiller aspirin originates from willow bark. Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, when he noticed that the mould Penicillium had killed the bacteria growing on an agar plate around it.

Today most new drugs are synthesised (made) by chemists working in the pharmaceutical industry. However, the starting point for a new drug may still be a chemical extracted from a plant or microorganism. Chemists may then change its structure to make it more effective or to reduce side effects, and produce it in large quantities.

New medical drugs have to be tested and trialled before they are used, to check that they are safe and effective. Drugs are extensively tested for three things: toxicity (is it harmful?), efficacy (does it work?) and dose (how much should be given?). Testing happens in two main stages: preclinical testing and clinical trials.

Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals. Testing on cells and tissues shows whether the drug has the expected effect and whether it damages cells. Testing on live animals shows how the drug works in a whole body, including its effects on different organs. Many drugs fail at this stage because they are toxic or do not work.

Clinical trials use healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the trial to healthy volunteers, to check that it is safe and to look for side effects. If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out on patients who have the disease, to find out whether the drug works and to find the optimum (best) dose.

In double blind trials, patients are randomly split into groups. Some patients are given the drug and some are given a placebo, which looks like the drug but does not contain it. Neither the doctors nor the patients know who has received a placebo and who has received the drug until the trial is complete. This stops the results being affected by what patients or doctors expect, so the effect of the drug itself can be measured fairly.

When the trial is complete, the results are written up and published only after scrutiny by peer review. This means other independent scientists who are experts in the field check the method, data and conclusions. Peer review helps to prevent false claims and makes sure the conclusions are valid before doctors rely on them.
keyFacts: Digitalis (a heart drug) originates from foxgloves.
Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.

How well a drug works, that is, whether it produces the effect it is meant to.
The amount of a drug given and how often it is given.

workedExamples.title: Analysing double blind trial results
workedExamples.question: In a double blind trial, 600 patients were given a new drug and 600 patients were given a placebo. 420 patients in the drug group and 150 in the placebo group showed improvement. Calculate the percentage of each group that improved and state what the results suggest.
steps: Some patients improved on the placebo, which shows the placebo effect or natural recovery.
The drug group improved much more (70% compared with 25%), so the improvement is due to the drug.
workedExamples.answer: 70% of the drug group and 25% of the placebo group improved, so the drug is effective.

workedExamples.title: Ordering the stages
workedExamples.question: Put these stages in the correct order: testing on patients to find the optimum dose; testing on cells and tissues; testing on healthy volunteers with very low doses; testing on live animals; peer review and publication.
steps: Preclinical testing comes first, in a laboratory: cells and tissues, then live animals.
Clinical trials come next: healthy volunteers receive very low doses to check safety.
If safe, trials on patients find whether it works and the optimum dose.
Finally results are checked by peer review before publication.
workedExamples.answer: Cells and tissues → live animals → healthy volunteers (low doses) → patients (optimum dose) → peer review and publication.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a dose
workedExamples.question: Clinical trials show the optimum dose of a drug is 2.5 mg per kg of body mass. Calculate the dose for a patient with a mass of 64 kg.
steps: Dose = dose per kg × body mass

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think clinical trials start by giving patients a full dose of the new drug.
misconceptions.right: In fact trials start with very low doses given to healthy volunteers to check safety. The optimum dose is found in later trials on patients.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a placebo is a weaker version of the drug.
misconceptions.right: In fact a placebo contains no drug at all. It just looks like the real drug.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'double blind' means the patients do not know which group they are in.
misconceptions.right: In fact that is single blind. In a double blind trial neither the patients nor the doctors know who has the drug until the trial is complete.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think preclinical testing is done on humans.
misconceptions.right: In fact preclinical testing is done in a laboratory on cells, tissues and live animals. Humans are only involved in clinical trials.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all modern drugs come straight from plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry, although the starting point may be a plant chemical.

realWorld: Digitalis from foxgloves (now made as digoxin) is still used to treat heart failure and irregular heartbeat by slowing and strengthening the heartbeat.
Aspirin, based on a chemical from willow bark, is used as a painkiller and in low doses to reduce the risk of blood clots.
Covid-19 vaccines went through preclinical testing and large double blind clinical trials with placebo groups before approval; results were peer reviewed and published.
Scientists still search rainforests and soil microorganisms for new chemicals that could become drugs.
examTips: Learn the three things drugs are tested for: toxicity, efficacy and dose. Many marks come from naming these.
Always say 'very low doses' are used at the start of clinical trials and that later trials find the 'optimum dose'.
When explaining double blind trials, state who does not know (both doctors and patients) AND why (to avoid bias from expectations).
Explain why a placebo is used: to compare with the drug group, so any improvement caused by the drug can be distinguished from the placebo effect.
Match the drug to its source: digitalis from foxgloves, aspirin from willow, penicillin from Penicillium mould (Fleming).
summary: Digitalis came from foxgloves, aspirin from willow and penicillin from Penicillium mould.
Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists, sometimes starting from a plant chemical.
Drugs are tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose.
Preclinical testing uses cells, tissues and live animals.
Clinical trials start with very low doses on healthy volunteers, then patients to find the optimum dose.
Double blind trials with a placebo stop bias.
Results are published only after peer review.

questions.question: Which drug originates from foxgloves?
markScheme: 1 mark: Digitalis
questions.explanation: Digitalis, a heart drug, comes from foxgloves. Aspirin comes from willow and penicillin from a mould.

questions.question: Aspirin originates from which organism?
markScheme: 1 mark: Willow
questions.explanation: The painkiller aspirin is based on a chemical found in willow bark.

questions.question: Who discovered penicillin?
markScheme: 1 mark: Alexander Fleming
questions.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin from Penicillium mould. Semmelweis promoted hand washing, Jenner developed vaccination and Pasteur worked on microorganisms and vaccines.

questions.question: What is a placebo?
options: A weaker dose of the drug
A substance that looks like the drug but contains no drug
A drug that has already passed trials
A drug given to animals in preclinical testing
markScheme: 1 mark: A substance that looks like the drug but contains no drug
questions.explanation: A placebo contains no active drug. It is given to a comparison group so that the drug's real effect can be measured.

questions.question: Which is used in preclinical testing?
markScheme: 1 mark: Cells, tissues and live animals
questions.explanation: Preclinical testing is laboratory testing on cells, tissues and live animals. Humans are only used in clinical trials.

questions.question: Why are very low doses given at the start of a clinical trial?
options: To check the drug is safe
Because the patients are very ill
markScheme: 1 mark: To check the drug is safe
questions.explanation: Low doses reduce harm if the drug turns out to be toxic in humans. The optimum dose is found in later trials.

questions.question: In a double blind trial, who knows which patients receive the drug before the trial is complete?
markScheme: 1 mark: Neither doctors nor patients
questions.explanation: Double blind means both the doctors and the patients are 'blind' to who has the drug until the trial is complete.

questions.question: What does 'efficacy' of a drug mean?
options: How much of the drug to give
How cheap the drug is to make
markScheme: 1 mark: How well the drug works
questions.explanation: Efficacy is whether the drug works. Toxicity is how harmful it is, and dose is how much to give.

questions.question: A drug company publishes a press release claiming a new drug works, before the results have been peer reviewed. Why should doctors be cautious?
options: The results have not been checked by independent experts
The drug has not been synthesised by chemists
Peer review is only needed for plant-based drugs
The drug has not been tested on placebos
markScheme: 1 mark: The results have not been checked by independent experts
questions.explanation: Peer review lets other scientists check the method and conclusions. Without it, the claims might be biased or invalid, especially as the company profits from the drug.

questions.question: In a trial, 30% of the placebo group and 32% of the drug group improved. What is the best conclusion?
options: The placebo is more effective than the drug
The drug has little or no effect beyond the placebo effect
markScheme: 1 mark: The drug has little or no effect beyond the placebo effect
questions.explanation: The two groups improved by almost the same amount, so most of the improvement is not caused by the drug. The data say nothing about toxicity.

questions.question:
In a clinical trial, 600 patients were given a new drug. 420 of these patients showed improvement.
Calculate the percentage of patients in this group who improved.

The optimum dose of a drug is 2.5 mg per kg of body mass.
Calculate the dose for a patient with a mass of 64 kg.
markScheme: 1 mark: 160 (mg)
questions.explanation: Multiply the dose per kg by the body mass: 2.5 × 64 = 160 mg.

questions.question:
A company screened 10 000 chemicals as possible new drugs. Only 5 of them passed preclinical testing and entered clinical trials.
Calculate the percentage of chemicals that entered clinical trials.
questions.explanation: 5 ÷ 10 000 = 0.0005, and × 100 gives 0.05%. Most chemicals fail early because they are toxic or not effective.

questions.question:
In a double blind trial, 420 out of 600 patients given a drug improved, and 150 out of 600 patients given a placebo improved.
Calculate the difference between the percentage improvement in the drug group and in the placebo group, in percentage points.
markScheme: 1 mark: drug group 70%
1 mark: placebo group 25%
1 mark: difference = 45 (percentage points)
questions.explanation: Drug: 420 ÷ 600 × 100 = 70%. Placebo: 150 ÷ 600 × 100 = 25%. 70 − 25 = 45 percentage points. This difference is the improvement due to the drug rather than the placebo effect.

questions.question: Name the three things that new drugs are tested for.
markScheme: 1 mark: toxicity
1 mark: efficacy
1 mark: dose
questions.explanation: Drugs are checked to see if they are harmful (toxicity), if they work (efficacy) and how much should be given (dose).

questions.question: Name the organism that penicillin was discovered from.
markScheme: 1 mark: Penicillium (mould)
questions.explanation: Fleming noticed that Penicillium mould killed bacteria growing near it on an agar plate.

questions.question: Name the two groups of people who are used in clinical trials.
markScheme: 1 mark: healthy volunteers
1 mark: patients (people with the disease)
questions.explanation: Healthy volunteers are given very low doses first to test safety; patients are then used to test whether the drug works and to find the optimum dose.

questions.question: Explain why a group of patients in a clinical trial is given a placebo.
acceptedAnswers: see if improvement is due to drug
markScheme: 1 mark: to act as a control / for comparison with the drug group
1 mark: to show whether any improvement is due to the drug and not the placebo effect (patients feeling better because they think they are being treated)
questions.explanation: Some patients improve just because they believe they are being treated. Comparing with a placebo group shows the real effect of the drug.

questions.question: Most new drugs are made by chemists. Explain why plants are still important in drug discovery.
markScheme: 1 mark: the starting point for a new drug may be a chemical extracted from a plant
1 mark: chemists can then modify/synthesise it in the laboratory (e.g. aspirin from willow)
questions.explanation: Even though most drugs are synthesised, many are based on chemicals first found in plants.

questions.question: Explain why drugs are tested on live animals as well as on cells and tissues during preclinical testing.
markScheme: 1 mark: cells and tissues do not show the effect on a whole organism
1 mark: animals show how the drug affects different organs/body systems and possible side effects
questions.explanation: A drug may be safe for isolated cells but harm an organ such as the liver or kidneys in a whole body.

questions.question: Describe what is meant by peer review and why it is used.
markScheme: 1 mark: results are checked by other (independent) scientists/experts before publication
1 mark: to check the method and conclusions are valid / prevent false or biased claims
questions.explanation: Results of drug trials are published only after scrutiny by peer review, which helps ensure they can be trusted.

questions.question: Explain why a double blind trial gives more valid results than a trial in which the doctors know which patients receive the drug.
markScheme: 1 mark: patients who know they have the drug may feel better because of their expectations (placebo effect)
1 mark: doctors who know might treat patients differently or interpret/record symptoms in a biased way
1 mark: so in a double blind trial any difference between the groups is due to the drug only
questions.explanation: Removing knowledge from both sides removes two sources of bias, so the results measure only the effect of the drug.

questions.question: Suggest why a placebo is not given to patients in some trials for drugs to treat a serious illness. Suggest what could be used instead.
markScheme: 1 mark: it would be unethical because patients on the placebo would be denied treatment and could become worse/die
1 mark: the new drug is compared with the existing best treatment instead
questions.explanation: Withholding treatment from a seriously ill patient is not acceptable, so the comparison group receives the current standard drug.

questions.question: A drug passed preclinical tests on animals but caused serious side effects in healthy volunteers. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: animal bodies are not identical to human bodies
1 mark: so a drug may be broken down / act differently in humans and cause effects not seen in animals
questions.explanation: This is why clinical trials start with very low doses: animal results do not guarantee safety in humans.

questions.question: State the type of drug that digitalis is.
markScheme: 1 mark: a heart drug
questions.explanation: Digitalis, from foxgloves, is used to treat heart conditions.

questions.question: Describe how a double blind clinical trial is carried out.
markScheme: Indicative content: patients with the disease are used; randomly divided into two groups; one group given the drug; other group given a placebo that looks the same but contains no drug; neither patients nor doctors know who has which until the trial is complete; similar numbers/ages/sex in each group; results of the groups compared at the end.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description including placebo group and the fact that neither doctors nor patients know.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. some get the drug and some do not.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The two defining features are the placebo comparison group and that neither doctors nor patients know who has which.

questions.question: Describe the process of discovery and development of a new medicine, from finding a possible drug to it being used by doctors.
markScheme: Indicative content: possible drug may be extracted from a plant/microorganism or synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry; tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose; preclinical testing in a laboratory on cells and tissues; then on live animals; clinical trials on healthy volunteers with very low doses to check safety/side effects; if safe, further trials on patients to check it works and find the optimum dose; double blind trials with a placebo; neither doctors nor patients know who has the drug; results peer reviewed before publication; then drug can be licensed and prescribed.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, logically sequenced description of discovery, preclinical testing, clinical trials (low dose, optimum dose, double blind/placebo) and peer review.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): description of preclinical and clinical stages with some detail but limited sequence or missing key points.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. 'it is tested on animals then people'.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The best answers give the stages in order and add the detail of each stage: what is tested, who or what it is tested on, and how bias is avoided.

questions.question: A new painkiller was tested. Group A (200 patients) received the drug and 150 reported less pain. Group B (200 patients) received a placebo and 60 reported less pain. Evaluate whether the drug is effective and whether the trial was well designed.
markScheme: Indicative content: drug group 75% improved, placebo group 30% improved; drug group improved much more, so the drug appears effective; some placebo improvement shows the placebo effect, so comparison was needed; large, equal group sizes increase confidence; should be double blind and randomised; groups should be matched (age, sex, severity); 'reported less pain' is subjective so blinding is especially important; should be repeated/peer reviewed; data say nothing about side effects or toxicity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): uses the data (percentages) to reach a conclusion and gives at least one strength and one limitation of the design.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement that the drug works or a single comment on design.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Evaluate questions need a judgement backed by data (75% vs 30%) and comments on both strengths and weaknesses of the method.
